notes.meaning: Jesus compares God's kingdom to a master who goes out early in the morning to hire day laborers for his grape vineyard. God is the great householder who calls people into His church and service. He graciously provides work and cares for His people rather than needing anything from them.

A denarius was the standard daily pay for a working man in Roman times. The owner and the first group of workers agreed on this fair wage before they headed out to the fields. Their agreement was open and completely normal for a regular workday.

The landowner visits the marketplace at nine in the morning, at noon, and again at three in the afternoon, finding more men with no work. He sends each group into the vineyard, promising to pay them whatever is fair and right. Unlike the first group, these laborers go to work simply trusting the owner's fairness without a set contract.

With only one hour left before sunset, the master finds still more men standing around. They had been waiting all day, but nobody had offered them a job. The master hires them immediately, showing that God welcomes willing workers even late in life.

When evening comes at six o'clock, the owner obeys the Old Testament command to pay laborers before the night begins. He instructs his manager to begin paying the workers starting from the last ones hired up to the first. This unusual order sets the stage for a lesson in divine generosity.

The men who worked for only one hour receive a full denarius, which was an entire day's pay. Watching this, the workers who arrived at dawn assume they will receive extra pay for their long shift. However, each of them also receives the single denarius they had originally agreed to earn.

The workers hired first begin to grumble against the householder as soon as they get their money. They feel insulted that the latecomers, who worked an easy hour in the cool evening, are treated as equals with those who endured the scorching sun and heavy toil all day long. Their complaint reveals a self-righteous attitude toward God's goodness to others.

The landowner calmly answers their spokesman, calling him a friend and pointing out that no promise was broken. The worker received every cent agreed upon, so no injustice was done to him. The owner tells him to take his wages and go, since the choice to bless the last man was the owner's free choice.

The owner asks if he is not allowed to spend his own money however he wishes. In ancient Jewish culture, an 'evil eye' was a common phrase for a jealous and greedy heart. The complainers were angry not because they were mistreated, but simply because the master chose to be generous to someone else.

Jesus concludes that those who seem last in human eyes will end up first, and those who seem first will end up last. God does not measure heavenly rewards by human seniority, earthly status, or boasting. Those who come to Christ late or seem least notable will receive the full joy of eternal life by His grace.

As Jesus walks toward Jerusalem for the Passover, He leads the Twelve away from the traveling crowds to speak with them privately. He knew the terrible events waiting for Him in the city and wanted to prepare His closest followers. This private warning was meant to strengthen their faith for the shock of His death.

Jesus gives a startlingly detailed prophecy about what will happen to Him in Jerusalem. He explains that the Jewish ruling priests and teachers will condemn Him to death and hand Him over to the Roman authorities. These Gentiles would mock Him, beat Him with whips, and execute Him on a cross, but on the third day He would be raised back to life.

Salome, the mother of the disciples James and John, kneels before Jesus to ask for a special favor. She asks that her two sons be given the two seats of greatest power and glory, on His right and left hand, when He rules His kingdom. The family still expected an earthly government filled with political titles and royal court honors.

Jesus replies that they do not realize what they are asking. In the Bible, drinking a 'cup' often means taking in a deep share of sorrow and suffering. The two brothers boldly claim they are able to bear that trial, failing to see their own weakness and the bitter agony that lay ahead.

Jesus assures the brothers that they will indeed share in His sufferings, which later came true through persecution and martyrdom. However, He explains that the highest seats of honor cannot be given out as personal favors to please ambitious followers. Those places belong to whoever God the Father has prepared them for in His eternal plan.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary explains that Christ answers in His human role as a servant, because as God He shares all authority with the Father to prepare and give the heavenly thrones.

notes.meaning: The other ten disciples are furious when they hear about the request made by James and John. Their anger came from their own selfish desire to be first in the kingdom. The dispute showed that pride and jealousy were still active in the hearts of all the apostles.

Jesus calls the whole group together to correct their false ideas about power. He reminds them that pagan rulers govern by throwing their weight around, bossing their subjects, and showing off their power. The kingdom of God has a completely different spirit and must never be run like a worldly empire.

Jesus turns normal worldly ideas of greatness upside down. Anyone who wants to be truly great in His kingdom must become a helper to everyone else. The person who desires the first place must take the lowest position and act like a servant to all.

Jesus points to His own life as the ultimate model of humble service. A 'ransom' means a price paid to buy freedom for a captive, and an 'atonement' is the way God and sinners are brought back together in peace. Jesus did not come expecting royal treatment, but gave His very life to pay the price to set sinners free.

differ.view: Some Baptists hold that Christ died as an effective ransom specifically for the elect, paying the exact debt for those God chose for salvation.
Methodists hold that Christ provided a ransom for all people everywhere, with the word 'many' describing the vast multitude of people who benefit from His one sacrifice.

notes.meaning: A large crowd tags along as Jesus and His disciples walk out of the city of Jericho. Even though Jesus was on His way to the cross, He stayed approachable and ready to show mercy. The crowd followed Him, eager to hear His teaching and see His works.

Two blind men sitting by the road hear the noise of the passing crowd and realize that Jesus is near. They immediately shout out, calling Him Lord and 'Son of David,' a title showing their faith that He was the promised Savior. They do not plead their own good works, but simply beg for His mercy.

The people in the crowd scold the blind men and tell them to keep quiet, treating them as an annoying nuisance to the Master. Instead of staying silent, the men shout all the louder for help. Their stubborn persistence shows how desperately they wanted the Savior's help.

Jesus stops walking and calls the two men over to Him. He asks them what they want Him to do, giving them the chance to state their need publicly before the crowd. They do not ask for spare coins, but specifically beg for their eyesight to be restored.

Filled with deep compassion, Jesus touches the blind men's eyes, and their sight returns in that very second. Having received their healing, they immediately begin following Jesus down the road as grateful disciples. Their lives became a living witness to His power and mercy.
